newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Hang Lung half-yr net seen lacklustre.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Hang Lung half-yr net seen lacklustre.

text.p: Hang Lung Development Co Ltd is expected to post lacklustre 1996/97 half-year results, with profit growth underperforming other major Hong Kong property developers as it books fewer sales, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Hang Lung does not have too many properties ready for sale. It has fewer projects (than other major developers)," Daiwa Securities analyst Eric Yuen said.

Analysts generally expect little shine in the property developer's interim results, scheduled to be released on Thursday, based on their forecasts for full-year 1996/97 ending June 30. Few analysts have forecast interim estimates.

The market on average tips Hang Lung's full-year 1996/97 net profit to grow 5.0 percent to HK$2.40 billion (US$310 million), according to the latest edition of Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory.
Earnings per share are seen rising 4.0 percent to HK$1.76.

Yuen, who anticipated a 10 percent increase in the firm's full-year net, said its expected growth rate is lower than the estimated growth at most major Hong Kong blue-chip developers, seen to be at least 20 percent in the same period.
He attributed Hang Lung's below-par forecast growth mainly to the limited number of developments it has for sale during the territory's ongoing property market boom.
HSBC James Capel property analyst Nicholas Wong noted that the firm had bought land at high prices and its output was restricted by an insufficient land bank.
Analysts have long criticised Hang Lung's land bank as being inadequate. The company has pledged to embark on an aggressive HK$6 billion land acquisition programme in calendar 1997.
The developer's net profit grew 5.31 percent to HK$2.28 billion in 1995/96.

Yuen noted that contributions from its 55 percent-held Amoy Properties Ltd, which develops investment properties and usually accounts for 40 to 60 percent of Hang Lung's net earnings, would help improve the parent's profit in 1996/97.
He tipped the unit's 1996/97 attributable profit to rise 21 percent, buoyed by property disposals. Analysts on average estimated HK$1.71 billion, representing a 8.0 percent increase.
Hotel owner and operator Grand Hotel Holdings Ltd, a Hang Lung subsidiary which contributes about five percent to its profit, is expected to post a satisfactory growth, analysts said.
"Its growth will not be bad," Yuen said. Hang Lung owns about 68 percent of Grand Hotel's A shares and about 63 percent of its B shares.
Analysts expect the hotel firm to post 18 percent growth in net profit to HK$250.6 million for 1996/97, with earnings per share tipped to jump 19 percent to HK$0.37.
The hotel industry in Hong Kong benefited from a surge in arrivals in 1996.
Hang Lung shares were down HK$0.55 to HK$14.40 at Tuesday's midsession.
